newsitem.title: USA: Four nations agree to continue Korea talks.
newsitem.headline: Four nations agree to continue Korea talks.

text.p: Famine-stricken North Korea and the United States, South Korea and China agreed on Wednesday to continue their talks aimed at clearing the way for negotiations on a permanent peace agreement on the divided Korean peninsula.
The preparatory talks, which began on Tuesday in New York, have a limited purpose -- to set a date, time, place and agenda for the opening of formal negotiations, probably in September.

"The talks so far have been useful and the four parties have agreed to continue their discussions on Thursday afternoon," a U.S. State Department official said. "They agreed to consult with their capitals on the discussions so far."

The ultimate goal was to replace the fraying armistice from the 1950-1953 Korean War with a more durable agreement, possibly in the form of a treaty. China was communist North Korea's ally in the conflict and the United States supported the capitalist South.
All four nations are parties to the armistice, which ended the fighting but did not technically end the war on the Korean peninsula, the last flashpoint of the Cold War.

U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam proposed the four-nation talks more than a year ago. It took months of discussions between Washington, Seoul and Pyongyang to reach the stage where China was also involved.
The meetings on Tuesday and Wednesday marked an important phase in the complex relationship between the four countries because it was the first time representatives of China had joined the talks.

Although no agreements were announced after the two days of meetings at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs, North Korea's continued engagament was probably a positive sign.
In Washington, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said, "I think we had a good opening day. I think that this is going to be a discussion that we carry on for some time."
She said the United States would not consider a North Korean request to withdraw U.S. troops from the demilitarized zone on the Korean peninsula.
"We are not going to do that. This is the last area of the Cold War," Albright said.

Officials from the delegations of China and North Korea declined comment Wednesday, but South Korean delegation head Song Young Shik, a deputy minister of Foreign Affairs, said the atmosphere was "friendly and productive".

One of the main obstacles in bringing the Pyongyang government to the table has been its demand for food aid. The isolated Stalinist state has been struck by famine, drought and potential economic collapse.
U.N. agencies said on Monday that the drought had devasted 70 percent of the country's maize crop. The agencies said even heavy rainfall would not be enough to alleviate the drought.
Some reports have likened the disaster to the famine in Ethiopia in the 1980s. Some 22 million of North Korea's 24 million people rely on their government for food.
The United States and South Korea sought to keep food aid out of the peace talks, but Pyongyang raised the matter in previous meetings during the past year.

"The United States is not linking the issue of food to these talks," a senior State Department official said. Albright said on Wednesday that Washington was considering sending additional food for famine victims.
The United Nations World Food Programme made a fresh appeal last month for $46 million in food aid for North Korea in addition to an earlier request of $95.5 million.

In a series of conciliatory steps on the eve of the New York talks, Pyongyang on Monday handed over the remains of four U.S. soldiers killed in the war and the two Koreas linked up their public telephone lines for the first time since 1945. The Red Cross of South Korea also announced food supplies to the North.
